articles.title: Female Perversions review – Tilda Swinton searches for erotic adventures in rework of Madame Bovary
articles.summary: The actor’s 1996 first US film, as a lawyer trying to manage her complicated love life and traumatic fantasies, marked her out as a screen presence like no other. Tilda Swinton made her US debut 30 years ago with this insouciant, startling, experimental adventure in eroticism and neuroticism.
body: Streitfeld’s fictional reworking does not focus on Emma Bovary. Instead Swinton plays a character called Eve, a brilliant, beautiful – and single – lawyer with an elegant, angular style; she is as graceful and sometimes comically clumsy as a baby giraffe. Eve is having a passionate affair with a hunky seismologist called John (Clancy Brown), an amusing metaphor for the quake-level sex they’re having. She is also deeply attractive and attracted to women, yet also assailed by traumatised fantasies or flashbacks of something in her past; there are terrible lurches of guilt or fear, abuse, loss, self-harm or impostor syndrome.
points: The actor’s 1996 first US film, as a lawyer trying to manage her complicated love life and traumatic fantasies, marked her out as a screen presence like no other.

articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.summary: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind?
body: The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.”

He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interested in the world of mystery and, I want to say supernatural, but dimensions that are intangible, by studying something like sleep paralysis.”

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a lotion to cure autumn dryness – and relieve eczema sufferers’ sore skin
articles.summary: Bioderma’s new eczema lotion will be comforting for anyone with dry skin. Plus another brilliant problem solving mosituriser. I spent much of my childhood basted in crude, heavy-duty emollient creams and grim bath oils.
body: Although unctuous emollients are necessary to protect a compromised skin barrier, they have a habit of just “sitting” there greasily, refusing to sink in or curtail the itch. The French pharmaceutical brand Bioderma is finally advancing the conversation. Its extensive research into eczema, as well as a recent study of 500 sufferers (about one in five children and one in 10 adults struggle with the condition), were presented as a breakthrough in eczema care at last month’s EADV (European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology) conference in Vienna.

Bioderma believes that eczema-compromised skin does not crave mere generic emollients, but lacks a precise combination of 15 lipids. The brand has sought to replace them with a new product, Atoderm AD Intensive Baume (£26), which is patented and approved for use on babies too. Trial results showed the “balm” (misnomer – it’s a thick lotion) soothed itching from the first second of application, and reduced the urge to scratch by 88%.
points: Bioderma’s new eczema lotion will be comforting for anyone with dry skin.

articles.title: Mini record player on track for No 1 in Christmas toy parade
articles.summary: Industry experts pick out tiny turntable as one of their ‘15 hottest toys’ for the festive season. A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn.
body: The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season.

The Mini Brands record player taps into the huge market for collectible toys. Part of the appeal is the 45 mini records to collect, ranging from Billie Eilish’s Birds of a Feather to Neil Diamond’s Sweet Caroline. The discs are sold separately in £8 “blind balls” with part of the attraction being the mystery of which songs are inside.

The trend for miniature products comes because making something smaller “makes it feel cuter”, suggests Melissa Symonds, executive director of UK toys at market research company Circana. While adults enjoyed the novelty, she suggested that children would relish acting out playing records in the same way that their parents did.

The record player is unlikely to satisfy high-end audiophiles, however, because the “vinyl” isn’t real. Instead, the discs contain a chip that activates a 30-second clip from the player’s internal memory.

articles.title: Show Us the Receipts: What a Corporate Employee, a Stylist, and a Content Creator Bought This Month
articles.summary: We asked three stylish people in or adjacent to the fashion industry to chronicle one month of their fashion consumption—and to note what was purchased at full price, discounted, and gifted.
body: Welcome to Show Us the Receipts, our recurring column on what fashion people really buy and spend.

Money remains taboo in almost every corner of life, but in fashion, dollars and cents can take on an especially complex dimension—from both inside and out. With a high buy-in to the luxury market and wages that don’t often allow professionals access to the goods offered by their own industry, we often find ourselves wondering how, exactly, our contemporaries afford their wardrobes. Do they come from generational wealth? Are they on every PR gifting list known to man? Are they savvy sale shoppers and bargain hunters? Or are they just really shrewd budgeters?
This month, a corporate employee at a luxury house, a stylist, and a content creator all offered Vogue a peek at their receipts.

articles.title: At This New Retreat on a Windswept Estonian Island, You Can Experience Five Seasons of Wellness
articles.summary: On the remote Baltic outpost of Hiiumaa Island, the newly opened Eha Retreat pairs cold plunges, bog peat body masks, and beehive meditation sessions with a sleek Nordic design philosophy.
body: You’ve heard of spring, summer, fall, and winter. But what about viies aastaaeg? Across the islands of western Estonia in late March, as the ice thaws and the Baltic mists shift, a micro-season is created—one that Eha, a new retreat on the remote island of Hiiumaa which opened in early October, has termed “springrise” and placed at the center of its “five seasons” wellness philosophy. “Hiiumaa has its own rhythm,” says the Tallinn-born Eva Maran, who has spent the past five years developing Eha alongside her partner, the Singaporean-Estonian entrepreneur Sonny Aswani. “Nothing can be forced.”

articles.title: Always-Sunny San Diego Keeps Getting Better—Here's How to Explore
articles.summary: The new hotels and restaurants to know about, plus things to do and neighborhood guides.
body: San Diego's calendar of sunny days, endless string of beaches on which to enjoy them, and family-friendly attractions have long drawn visitors year-round to the city and surrounding county. Lately new, design-centric hotels and a growing slate of destination restaurants are joining the enduring pleasures to create an era of vibrancy for all travelers to enjoy.

With walkable streets, vintage shops, and craft breweries, North Park and Hillcrest districts are also rich in restaurants and nightlife. In North Park, sample French bistro fare at the Smoking Goat or Iberian seafood at Mabel's Gone Fishing, then end at listening bar Part Time Lover. Hillcrest, the epicenter of the LGBTQ+ scene, is home to the Brass Rail, the city's first gay bar, and Urban Mo's Bar and Grill, a beloved hub.

Soaring sea cliffs and palm-lined boulevards are only part of La Jolla's appeal—visit arts and culture institutions like La Jolla Playhouse and the Museum of Contemporary Art, and try classic restaurants such as George's at the Cove or The Marine Room for lunch with a view.
points: The new hotels and restaurants to know about, plus things to do and neighborhood guides.

articles.title: Zoë Kravitz Is Back on the Red Carpet, Going for Gold, And Baring Her Abs
articles.summary: Stepping out for the “How To Rob A Bank” premiere in New York City, Zoë Kravitz made a return to form care of Saint Laurent.
body: What does one wear to the premiere of a movie called How to Rob a Bank? If you’re Zoë Kravitz, it’s got to be something worth stealing. The actor made a glittering return to the red carpet in New York last night, attending the premiere of her new film alongside co-stars Nicholas Hoult and Pete Davidson. The actor opted for suitably decadent, gilded gold Saint Laurent ensemble, with plenty of skin on show—in one fell swoop, hitting two of her red carpet rules.

Kravitz wore a cropped, long-sleeved jacket in richly patterned gold brocade, with an embellished neckline and plush, dark brown faux-fur cuffs. Sitting low on her hips were matching straight-leg trousers, with intricate crystal embellishments and a sparkling floral buckle at the waistband. Barely-there metallic sandals, delicate earrings, and an undone updo with wispy tendrils framing her face finished things off. And there was a generous flash of those famously toned abs.

articles.title: Jolie Made the Showerhead a Beauty Staple. What’s Next?
articles.summary: Jolie’s new Filtered Handheld Showerhead marks the next chapter for the beauty-wellness brand, which has built a $65 million business around a single hero product.
body: A showerhead is not an obvious candidate for brand cachet. Yet Jolie has turned one of the bathroom’s most overlooked fixtures into a beauty-wellness product and a conversation piece. Through Erewhon drink collaborations, a Copenhagen Fashion Week art installation, and “Shower Thoughts”, its interview series featuring creatives and designers, the brand has made a long-ignored item newly desirable.

Nearly five years after launching with a single filtered showerhead, Jolie co-founder and CEO Ryan Babenzien is ready for the brand’s next phase. The beauty and wellness company, which is on track to generate $65 million in revenue in 2026, is introducing its second product on November 11: the Filtered Handheld Showerhead. Available in five of the brand’s signature colorways, including Modern Chrome, Brushed Gold and Vibrant Red, the handheld features a lightweight silhouette, a knurled aluminium handle and a magnetic docking system that allows it to snap into place.
points: Jolie’s new Filtered Handheld Showerhead marks the next chapter for the beauty-wellness brand, which has built a $65 million business around a single hero product.

articles.title: High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look
articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much.
body: Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.
